title: In a room of 23 people, a shared birthday is more likely than not
body: The trick is that birthdays get compared between every pair of people, not just against yours. With 23 people there are **253 possible pairs**, and each one is another chance for a match, so the probability of at least one shared birthday passes 50%: it's 50.7%. With 70 people it tops 99.9%. The same maths, known as the birthday attack, tells cryptographers how quickly two different inputs to a hash function are likely to collide.

slides.question: How many different pairs of people can you form from 23 people?
slides.explanation: 253 pairs: each of the 23 can pair with 22 others, and that counts every pair twice, so 23 × 22 ÷ 2 = 253.

slides.alt: Animation at a party: 23 guests drop onto a calendar of 365 days until two land on the same day, and 1,000 simulated parties fill a grid, about half with a match. Lines join every pair of guests, 253 in all, and a curve climbs to 50.7% at 23 people and 99.9% at 70.
slides.music: “Sunflower Dance Party” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: Why it feels wrong
slides.text: We tend to compare everyone's birthday with our own. With 22 other people, the chance that someone shares yours is only about 6%. But the others also get compared with each other, and those pairs are most of the 253.

slides.heading: Chance that at least two people share a birthday
slides.note: Assuming 365 equally likely birthdays and ignoring leap days.

slides.question: How many other people would it take for a better-than-even chance that one shares your own birthday?
slides.explanation: At least 253. Every comparison now has to involve you, so you need far more people. Curiously, it's the same number as the pairs among 23 people.

slides.heading: Real birthdays
slides.text: The maths assumes 365 equally likely birthdays and ignores leap days and twins. Real birthdays are a little uneven, which only makes a match more likely, but not by enough to matter: it still takes 23 people.
